newsitem.title: FRANCE: Frenchman fond of solo quests plans new adventure.
newsitem.headline: Frenchman fond of solo quests plans new adventure.

text.p: A Frenchman fond of risky solo adventures announced plans on Thursday to spend eight to 10 weeks 20 feet underwater in the Indian Ocean early next year, in a tiny submarine suspended from a floating support vessel.

"There are a lot of potential risks" in the mission including a threat of shark attacks, suffocation and pirates, said Guy Delage of Nantes, western France, who last year made a highly publicised solo swim across the Atlantic.
"You may laugh when someone brings up pirates, but it's not funny," he told a Paris news conference.

In an earlier adventure that fascinated France two years ago, Delage alternately swam and floated on a raft the 3,900 km (2,420 miles) from the Cape Verde Islands off the west coast of Africa to the Caribbean island of Barbados.

The eight-week swim which began in December 1994 was clouded by controversy over whether he had been unduly helped along by trade winds and sea currents, and whether the journey had been a genuine feat or a publicity stunt.
The 44-year-old Delage promised to conduct his new adventure more rigorously so as to make it useful both as a scientific mission and a personal challenge.
During his weeks floating in the Indian Ocean, steered only by the prevailing winds and currents, he will film and photograph marine life, grow algae and record data on the effects of his isolation.
The film and data will alll be beamed back to France via communications satellite for analysis by a waiting team of doctors and scientists.
One of the trip's sponsors hopes to use the data to establish a business cultivating edible algae in deep, warm water such as the Indian Ocean.

During the mission, to begin in mid-January and estimated to cost two million francs ($400,000), Delage said he would spend most of each day in the tiny submarine, observing through its large windows at 1.65 times normal atmospheric pressure.
Part of each day would be spent outside the submarine, taking photographs of marine life and collecting algae and plankton while using underwater breathing apparatus.

Delage would spend an hour or two each day on board the support vessel floating above the submarine at the ocean surface, equipped with electrical and communications gear, an air pump and algae cultivation facilities.

He would have no control over the precise length of the mission, saying it was in the hands of his support team of some 50 individuals back in France. The team includes scientists, doctors and a psychologist expert in the effects of isolation.
Should he run into trouble, he would have to rely on the same ocean rescue network available to any vessel, he said. He will have two self-inflating survival rafts in case of dire emergency.

Delage, who is married and has two children aged nine and five, has in the past raced sailing yachts and piloted ultra-light solo aircrafts. In 1991 he flew an ultra-light plane of his own design across the Atlantic in 26 hours.
